title: A Glasshouse for the Undertow
premise: Silas Halloran, once the conservatory's most promising pianist, returns five years after his public unraveling as the man who mops its floors. When the seaside house where his late mother taught him to play goes up for auction, he learns the buyer plans demolition, and that the auction's executor is Wren Calloway, his former duet partner and the person he loved without ever saying so. As Silas catalogues the house's contents for the estate sale, he is forced to confront the letter he never mailed and the truth about why he abandoned music. In the end, Silas plays the house's out-of-tune piano aloud one last time, confesses to Wren on the empty lawn, and lets the demolition proceed—carrying the music forward instead of the grief.
about_author: U. M. Blackwood is the pen name of a former conservatory archivist who spent a decade cataloguing other people's unfinished letters before writing her own. Her fiction explores the quiet violence of things left unsaid, and she lives within earshot of the sea.

chapters.title: The Mop and the Metronome
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Working nights as a janitor in the conservatory where he was once a prodigy, Silas avoids the practice rooms and the eyes of old teachers, finding strange peace in invisibility. When a flyer announces the auction of the Halloran house, his careful anonymity cracks. Emotional beat: the uneasy comfort of hiding, and the first tremor of what hiding has cost him.

chapters.title: Executor, Unknown
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. At the county office, Silas discovers Wren Calloway is handling the estate—his mother's old friend's daughter, his former duet partner, now a lawyer. Their first conversation is polite, precise, and devastating in what it doesn't say. He volunteers to inventory the house. Emotional beat: the shock of being seen again, and the reckless hope that comes with it.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Alone in the shuttered house, Silas catalogs objects: his mother's sheet music, a child's metronome, a drawer of unsent letters—including one in his own handwriting he never mailed. Flashbacks reveal his mother's illness and his final recital. Emotional beat: grief resurfacing as tenderness, and the dread of the letter's existence.

chapters.title: What Wren Kept
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren returns to town to close an estate she never wanted to administer, hiding her own history with the Hallorans—and with Silas. Finding the house untouched, she plays a recording of their teenage duet, then stops herself. She learns the buyer intends demolition. Emotional beat: her loyalty to the dead versus her hunger for the living truth.

chapters.title: The Buyer's Blueprints
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Silas meets the developer, a courteous man with demolition permits and no malice, and realizes no villain will save the house—only time. Wren and Silas work late cataloguing, and almost-speeches accumulate like dust. He nearly tells her about the letter; instead he tells her about the recital. Emotional beat: rising tension between confession and retreat.

chapters.title: Duet, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A conservatory fundraiser forces Silas and Wren into public view; a well-meaning colleague asks Silas to play, and he refuses in front of Wren, reviving the old story of his breakdown. Later, Wren confronts him: she heard him practice at midnight for weeks and never said. Emotional beat: loyalty revealed as its own kind of silence; the first open wound between them.

chapters.title: The Letter, Unsent
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Silas rereads his unsent letter—written at nineteen, confessing love and blame entangled—and understands his mother intercepted it, believing she was protecting his future. Fury and forgiveness arrive together. He asks Wren to extend the demolition date; she says she can't, or won't, and won't say why. Emotional beat: the cost of other people's protection.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren's secret surfaces: the demolition is her firm's commission, and she took it to prove she'd stopped orbiting Silas's tragedies. She walks the beach at the house, remembers the day his mother asked her to look after him, and decides loyalty to the dead cannot outrank truth to the living. Emotional beat: her breaking point, and her turn toward honesty.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Silas, POV, climax. On auction day, strangers buy his childhood in lots. Silas bids on the piano he cannot afford and loses it—then, before the crowd disperses, sits and plays the piece from their duet, badly and aloud, for the first time in five years. He tells Wren everything, out loud, in front of whoever remains. Emotional beat: public confession as both ruin and release.

chapters.title: Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, resolution. Demolition day: Wren arrives having bought the piano herself and left it in the conservatory's glass atrium, where Silas now teaches a Saturday class for adults who started too late. They stand on the lawn as the house comes down, saying goodbye properly, together. Emotional beat: belonging rebuilt not by preserving the past, but by carrying it forward.
